## Proof

Let $p(m)$ denote the number of partitions of $m$ (with $p(0)=1$). We compute each sum by exchanging the order of summation: instead of summing a quantity over partitions, we count *pairs* (partition, distinguished element).

**Computing $\sum f(p)$.**

$\sum f(p)$ counts the number of pairs $(p, \text{a specific occurrence of a }1\text{ in }p)$. Grouping these pairs by "which occurrence" — first 1, second 1, etc. — we get

$$\sum f(p) = \sum_{k\ge 1} \bigl(\text{number of partitions of } n \text{ containing at least } k \text{ ones}\bigr).$$

A partition of $n$ containing at least $k$ ones is, after removing those $k$ ones, exactly a partition of $n-k$. Hence the number of such partitions is $p(n-k)$. Summing over all $k$ with $1\le k\le n$:

$$\sum f(p) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} p(n-k) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} p(j). \tag{1}$$

**Computing $\sum g(p)$.**

$\sum g(p)$ counts the number of pairs $(p, \text{a distinct value } v \text{ appearing in } p)$. Grouping by the value $v$:

$$\sum g(p) = \sum_{v\ge 1} \bigl(\text{number of partitions of } n \text{ containing } v \text{ as a part}\bigr).$$

A partition of $n$ containing $v$ as a part is, after removing one copy of $v$, exactly a partition of $n-v$. (Removing one part of size $v$ from a partition of $n$ gives a partition of $n-v$, and conversely any partition of $n-v$ can be augmented by adding a part $v$ to give a partition of $n$ containing $v$.) Thus the number of such partitions is $p(n-v)$. Summing over all $v$ with $1\le v\le n$:

$$\sum g(p) = \sum_{v=1}^{n} p(n-v) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} p(j). \tag{2}$$

**Conclusion.**

Both (1) and (2) equal $\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} p(j)$, the total number of partitions of all integers from $0$ to $n-1$. Therefore

$$\sum_{p\vdash n} f(p) \;=\; \sum_{p\vdash n} g(p). \qquad\blacksquare$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
